item.title: Property sector ranks second for AI adoption as UK business use doubles
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK property sector has emerged as one of the country's leading industries in artificial intelligence adoption, with nearly half of real estate businesses now using AI tools, according to recent government data analysis. Research conducted by proptech firm Dwelly reveals that 45% of property businesses have implemented AI solutions, ranking the sector second only to information and communication (61%) in technology uptake.

Property Outpaces Finance in AI Adoption

The findings demonstrate significant growth in technology adoption within the real estate industry, which now leads more traditionally tech-focused sectors. Property's 45% adoption rate exceeds that of both financial services and business services, which stand at 39% each. This marks a notable shift in how the property sector approaches digital transformation, though the data doesn't differentiate between different types of real estate businesses.

Across all UK industries, AI usage has doubled in the past year, rising from 16% to 32% of businesses. The research also indicates changing attitudes towards artificial intelligence, with fewer firms considering the technology irrelevant to their operations - down from 51% to 38% over the same period.

From Basic Adoption to Operational Integration

While adoption rates are increasing, experts suggest many businesses are still in the early stages of implementation. Industry professionals note there's a significant difference between occasional administrative use of AI and fully integrating the technology into core business operations.

Sam Humphreys of Dwelly commented: "The real opportunity lies in moving beyond basic adoption and developing technology that can manage entire workflows, improve efficiency and enhance customer experiences." This perspective highlights the potential for more sophisticated applications beyond current implementations.

The research coincides with Dwelly's own expansion strategy, having completed ten acquisitions this year to grow its managed property portfolio to over 15,000 homes. Their approach demonstrates how technology adoption and business growth strategies are becoming increasingly intertwined in the property sector.

As AI becomes more prevalent across industries, the property sector's early adoption positions it well for potential efficiency gains and service improvements. However, the extent to which businesses leverage these technologies beyond basic functions may determine their competitive advantage in an increasingly digital marketplace.

item.title: Three letters that could transform estate agency and end CRM headaches
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A new technological development called Model Context Protocol (MCP) could revolutionise how estate agents and property professionals manage workflows, potentially solving long-standing CRM integration challenges. This innovation acts as a universal translator between different software systems, allowing seamless communication without the need for multiple custom integrations.

How MCP simplifies property management

Traditionally, property professionals have faced significant hurdles when trying to connect various PropTech solutions with their existing CRM systems. Each integration requires custom development, often proving costly and time-consuming. MCP eliminates this complexity by enabling different platforms to communicate directly through AI-powered language models like ChatGPT or Gemini.

For example, when arranging property inspections, users can now simply paste a spreadsheet of properties into their preferred AI interface or issue verbal instructions. The system automatically processes requests and returns confirmations without requiring manual dashboard access. This streamlined approach could save property managers considerable time on routine administrative tasks.

The potential impact on property transactions

Beyond simplifying day-to-day operations, MCP could transform the entire property transaction process. The technology enables different stakeholders – including solicitors, mortgage brokers and surveyors – to communicate more effectively through a standardised protocol. Given that communication breakdowns frequently cause transaction delays, this development might help accelerate the home moving process.

Industry observers note that despite its potential, awareness of MCP remains limited within government and regulatory circles. As the technology becomes more widely adopted, property professionals might wish to explore how it could enhance their service offering and operational efficiency.

Preparing for the MCP revolution

For estate agencies and property management firms considering adopting MCP solutions, the key requirement is having up-to-date software capable of running an MCP server. Early adopters are already demonstrating how the technology can reduce administrative burdens and improve client service.

As PropTech continues to evolve, MCP represents an important step towards creating a more connected, efficient property industry. While the full implications are still emerging, this innovation could fundamentally change how professionals interact with technology throughout the property lifecycle.

With communication being a persistent challenge in property transactions, solutions like MCP might finally provide the tools needed to create a smoother experience for all parties involved in the home moving process.

item.title: OneDome completes major acquisition
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

OneDome has strengthened its position in the mortgage advisory sector by acquiring a majority stake in Cornerstone Finance Group. The deal expands OneDome's combined mortgage distribution network to over 900 advisers, collectively arranging more than £15bn in annual lending. This follows the firm's acquisition of Mortgage Intelligence in 2022, continuing its strategic expansion in the financial services market.

Expanding mortgage advisory capabilities

Cardiff-based Cornerstone Finance Group brings 320 mortgage and protection advisers across 121 appointed representative firms into OneDome's growing network. While financial details remain undisclosed, the arrangement allows Cornerstone to maintain its brand identity, management team and operational independence. The firm will gain access to OneDome's technological platforms, product range and wider distribution channels as part of the agreement.

The acquisition forms part of OneDome's Growth Partners strategy, which supports mortgage brokers with technology solutions, lead generation services and specialist lending options. Advisers within the expanded network may also utilise OneDome's HomeBuyer Service – a fixed-price package combining mortgage advice with conveyancing and transaction support.

Technology-driven brokerage growth

OneDome founder and CEO Babek Ismayil commented on the evolving needs of modern mortgage brokers: "The next generation of successful brokerage businesses will require more than traditional network support. Increasingly, they'll need technological solutions, compelling consumer propositions, capital access and practical growth support alongside broader product offerings."

Cornerstone CEO Haydn Thomas highlighted how the partnership could benefit member firms: "This investment enables accelerated, sustainable growth for Cornerstone. Our advisers gain access to improved pricing through the OneDome network, alongside enhanced lead generation opportunities and greater technological resources."

The Cardiff office will continue as Cornerstone's specialist operational base while expanding its commercial finance activities. The deal reinforces OneDome's ambition to integrate mortgage advice with conveyancing and other property transaction services within a single group structure.

With this acquisition, OneDome solidifies its position as a significant player in the mortgage distribution sector, offering an increasingly comprehensive proposition for both advisers and homebuyers.

item.title: Over-65s hold £2.25tn in property wealth – but few are downsizing
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Homeowners aged 65 and over are sitting on a staggering £2.25tn in property wealth, according to recent research from Savills. This figure marks a dramatic increase compared to three decades ago, when older homeowners held just £232bn in housing equity. The rise reflects decades of house price growth and an ageing population, with older generations now accounting for a significant portion of the UK’s owner-occupied housing wealth. Despite this, relatively few are choosing to downsize, leaving much of this wealth tied up in property.

A Sharp Rise in Housing Wealth

The research highlights the extent to which property wealth has grown among older homeowners. Adjusted for inflation, the £2.25tn held by over-65s represents a 372% increase since 1995 and a 52% rise since 2010. This surge is partly due to the growing number of older homeowners, with households headed by someone aged 65 or over rising from 3.32 million in 1995 to 6.12 million in 2025. Average housing equity has also climbed sharply, increasing from £67,816 in 1995 to £353,539 in 2025.

Lucian Cook, head of residential research at Savills, commented, “The extraordinary increase in housing wealth held by older homeowners reflects three decades of house price growth and a significant demographic shift.” He added that this wealth remains largely concentrated in property until it is released through downsizing, later-life borrowing, or inheritance.

Downsizing Trends and Challenges

Despite the vast sums tied up in property, downsizing remains relatively uncommon among older homeowners. Savills estimates that just 131,200 households downsized during 2025–26, selling properties worth a combined £60.7bn. After purchasing replacement homes, these households released £20.8bn in equity. On average, downsizers sold their properties for £462,500 and bought new homes for £304,150.

Downsizers are more prevalent in higher-value markets, accounting for 33% of sellers disposing of properties worth over £1m. In contrast, they represented just 6.7% of sellers in the £250,000-and-under market. The reluctance to downsize is often driven by a shortage of suitable properties and the financial costs associated with moving, such as stamp duty and legal fees.

Regional Variations in Property Wealth

The South East leads the way in terms of property wealth among older homeowners, with £468bn tied up in housing equity. Around 942,000 households in the region are headed by someone aged 65 or over, reflecting the area’s popularity among retirees and its higher-than-average property values.

While downsizing offers a potential route to releasing equity, many older homeowners appear hesitant to take this step. As a result, much of the UK’s housing wealth remains concentrated in the hands of older generations, with implications for inheritance, later-life borrowing, and the wider property market.

For those considering downsizing, it could be worth exploring the options available, including the availability of suitable properties and the financial implications of moving. With the right planning, downsizing can be a practical way to unlock equity and enhance financial flexibility in later life.

item.title: Courts struggling to cope as possession claims rise
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Recent figures reveal a significant increase in possession claims across England and Wales, with the private rented sector (PRS) seeing a 21% year-on-year rise. This surge comes amidst growing pressures on the court system and coincides with the impending abolition of Section 21 'no fault' evictions under the Renters Reform Bill.

Court systems under pressure as eviction cases climb

Legal professionals and letting agents report mounting delays in possession cases as courts grapple with higher workloads. The current backlog means some landlords now face waits of several months before cases reach hearing dates, whilst tenants remain in uncertain circumstances during this period.

Several factors may be contributing to this situation:

  • Economic pressures making rent payments more difficult for some tenants
  • Landlords seeking possession before potential changes to eviction rules
  • Increased mortgage costs prompting some landlords to reconsider their portfolios

Section 21 changes on the horizon

The government's proposed Renters Reform Bill, currently progressing through Parliament, will abolish Section 21 notices - the mechanism allowing landlords to regain possession without stating a reason. Whilst intended to improve tenant security, the changes have sparked debate about their potential impact on the rental market.

Industry observers suggest some landlords may be initiating possession proceedings now to avoid navigating the new system later. Others highlight that legitimate grounds for eviction will remain under Section 8 procedures, albeit potentially requiring stronger evidence of tenant breaches.

For those involved in the rental market, it could be worth:

  • Reviewing tenancy agreements to ensure compliance with current regulations
  • Understanding the transitional period as reforms are implemented
  • Seeking professional legal advice regarding possession proceedings

As the proposed reforms continue their legislative journey, all parties in the private rented sector face a period of adjustment. The coming months may see further shifts in possession claim patterns as both landlords and tenants adapt to changing regulations and economic conditions.

item.title: Burnham cracks down on service charges
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Leaseholders in England and Wales are set to benefit from enhanced rights and protections under new government proposals aimed at tackling unfair service charges. The measures, announced by Housing Secretary Andy Burnham, seek to address longstanding concerns about opaque fees and poor management practices in the leasehold sector.

What’s Changing for Leaseholders?

The proposed reforms focus on increasing transparency and fairness in service charges, which cover maintenance, repairs, and other shared costs in leasehold properties. Under the new rules, landlords and managing agents will be required to provide detailed breakdowns of service charges, ensuring leaseholders understand exactly what they are paying for. Additionally, stricter guidelines will be introduced to prevent excessive or unjustified fees.

Leaseholders may also gain the right to challenge service charges more effectively through an independent tribunal. This could provide a stronger avenue for resolving disputes and holding landlords accountable for poor-quality services or unreasonable costs.

Why Are These Reforms Important?

Service charges have long been a contentious issue for leaseholders, with many reporting unclear billing practices and escalating costs. In some cases, homeowners have faced significant financial strain due to unexpected fees or substandard maintenance services. The new measures aim to address these issues by fostering greater accountability and fairness in the leasehold system.

For those considering purchasing a leasehold property, these changes could offer greater peace of mind. Enhanced transparency and stronger rights may make leasehold ownership a more attractive and manageable option for prospective buyers.

What Should Leaseholders Do Next?

Whilst the reforms are yet to be fully implemented, leaseholders may wish to familiarise themselves with their existing rights and responsibilities. Reviewing lease agreements and understanding the breakdown of current service charges could help homeowners identify any potential issues early on.

Borrowers might also consider seeking independent advice if they have concerns about their service charges or the management of their property. Organisations such as the Leasehold Advisory Service (LEASE) can provide valuable guidance and support.

These proposals represent a significant step forward in addressing the challenges faced by leaseholders. By promoting transparency and fairness, the reforms could help create a more balanced and efficient leasehold system for homeowners across the country.

item.title: Room rental hotspots revealed
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

The UK’s rental market continues to evolve, with certain areas emerging as hotspots for room rentals due to growing demand and rising prices. Recent data highlights Chesham and Stockport as two locations experiencing significant interest from tenants and landlords alike. These towns are proving to be attractive options for those looking to invest in rental properties or find affordable accommodation.

Chesham: A Growing Rental Hub

Situated in Buckinghamshire, Chesham has seen a surge in demand for room rentals. Its appeal lies in its proximity to London, making it a convenient option for commuters seeking more affordable living arrangements outside the capital. The town’s blend of rural charm and excellent transport links has made it a magnet for tenants, particularly young professionals and students.

Landlords in Chesham are also benefiting from rising rental prices, as competition among tenants drives up costs. For property investors, this could present an opportunity to capitalise on the increasing demand. However, it’s worth noting that whilst rental yields are growing, property prices in the area have also risen, potentially impacting overall returns.

Stockport: A Northern Gem

Stockport, located in Greater Manchester, has also emerged as a key player in the rental market. Known for its affordability and vibrant local economy, the town is attracting tenants who are priced out of nearby Manchester. With a range of amenities, good transport links, and a thriving community, Stockport offers a balanced lifestyle that appeals to a wide demographic.

For landlords, Stockport’s rental market offers promising yields, particularly as demand continues to outstrip supply. The town’s regeneration projects and investment in infrastructure have further boosted its appeal, making it an attractive option for those looking to expand their property portfolios.

What Does This Mean for Renters and Investors?

For tenants, these hotspots represent opportunities to secure affordable accommodation in areas with strong transport links and local amenities. However, rising rents in Chesham and Stockport mean that tenants may need to act quickly to secure the best deals.

For property investors, these locations could offer potential for strong rental yields and capital growth. However, it’s essential to conduct thorough research and consider factors such as property prices, local market conditions, and ongoing costs before making any investment decisions.

As the rental market continues to shift, Chesham and Stockport stand out as areas ripe with potential for both tenants and landlords. Whether seeking affordable accommodation or a promising investment opportunity, these towns are worth keeping an eye on.

item.title: Lettings profitable for eight in ten investors
item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

New research suggests that the vast majority of UK landlords are seeing positive returns from their property investments, with a significant proportion achieving substantial profits. The findings highlight the continued appeal of buy-to-let investments, despite recent challenges in the property market.

Strong Returns for Landlords

According to the latest data, an impressive 85% of landlords report making a profit from their lettings. This figure demonstrates the resilience of the buy-to-let sector, even amidst economic uncertainty and rising costs. Notably, 17% of landlords say they are achieving significant returns, indicating that well-managed property investments can still yield strong financial rewards.

Factors Influencing Profitability

Several factors may contribute to the profitability of buy-to-let investments. Location remains a key consideration, with properties in high-demand areas often commanding higher rental yields. Careful property selection, effective tenant management, and strategic financing decisions can also play a crucial role in maximising returns.

Landlords might also consider the potential benefits of longer-term tenancies, which can reduce void periods and associated costs. Additionally, maintaining properties to a high standard could help attract and retain quality tenants, further supporting profitability.

Challenges and Considerations

While the research paints a positive picture for many landlords, it’s important to acknowledge the challenges facing the sector. Rising interest rates, increased regulation, and higher maintenance costs have put pressure on some investors. Those considering entering the buy-to-let market may wish to carefully assess their financial position and seek professional advice to ensure they are well-prepared for potential hurdles.

Despite these challenges, the findings suggest that, for many, property investment remains a viable and potentially lucrative option. With careful planning and management, landlords could continue to achieve strong returns in the lettings market.

As with any investment, thorough research and a clear understanding of the risks and rewards are essential. Landlords and potential investors might find it valuable to stay informed about market trends and seek expert guidance to make well-informed decisions.

item.title: Microsoft outage delays property deals as estate agents resort to old-school tactics
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

A recent Microsoft outage caused delays in property transactions across the UK, forcing estate agents to resort to traditional communication methods to keep deals on track. The disruption, which affected services such as Outlook and Teams, highlighted the challenges faced by the property sector when reliant on digital platforms. Whilst many agencies adapted swiftly, others were forced to postpone transactions until the following week.

How Estate Agents Adapted

Estate agents across the country had to think creatively to overcome the communication challenges posed by the outage. Many turned to phone calls and direct conversations with solicitors and clients to ensure transactions progressed. Mitchells Estate Agency in Cumbria, for example, delayed two land transactions until early the following week, informing customers via Facebook of the disruption. Acorn Group, a larger property business, also experienced issues but managed to keep deals moving by using alternative channels and direct communication. Neil Louth, Group Executive Director at Acorn Group, praised his team’s initiative, stating that “good old-fashioned common sense” helped them navigate the situation.

Hamptons, another major estate agent, largely maintained normal operations despite the outage. Mary Beeton, Head of Sales at Hamptons, noted that solicitors took the initiative to resolve issues directly over the phone. Whilst the disruption was inconvenient, it demonstrated the resilience of the property sector in adapting to unexpected challenges.

Microsoft’s Response and Broader Implications

Microsoft apologised for the global outage, which affected users in over 70 countries. The technology giant attributed the disruption to a technical fault during a network capacity upgrade and confirmed it was not the result of a cyberattack. By Friday evening, some services had been restored, but Microsoft could not provide a definitive timeline for full recovery.

The incident has sparked broader concerns about the property industry’s reliance on major technology providers. Chand Chudasama, Chairman of Price Bailey, an accountancy and business advisory firm, warned of the risks associated with widespread cloud outages. He noted that resilience planning often assumes isolated failures, whereas cloud outages can have far-reaching consequences. This raises questions about how businesses, including estate agents, can safeguard against similar disruptions in the future.

Whilst the outage was temporary, it serves as a reminder of the importance of having contingency plans in place. Borrowers and homeowners involved in property transactions may wish to consider how such disruptions could potentially impact their own timelines and explore alternative communication methods with their agents or solicitors if needed.

For now, estate agents have demonstrated their ability to adapt, but the incident underscores the need for greater resilience in an increasingly digital-dependent property market.

item.title: Council rent arrears surge 57% as tenant debts mount
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

Council rent arrears across England have surged by 57% since 2019, with over four in ten social housing tenants now behind on payments, according to new research. The findings highlight growing financial pressures on both local authority landlords and tenants amid rising living costs.

Sharp rise in council rent debts

Freedom of Information data from 108 local authorities reveals the average council is now owed £2.96m in unpaid rent - up from £1.88m in 2019. The proportion of council-owned properties with rent arrears has climbed to 43%, compared to just 34% seven years earlier.

While the average debt per household has decreased slightly over the past year (down 2% to £674.62), the number of tenants falling behind has grown significantly. The 15% annual increase in affected households represents the steepest rise recorded since 2019.

Industry analysts suggest these patterns indicate financial strain is spreading more widely across social housing tenants, rather than being concentrated among those with particularly large individual debts.

Mounting pressures on tenants and councils

The research estimates total rent arrears across England's council housing stock could approach £675m if current trends continue. This comes as social housing rents continue rising alongside broader cost of living increases.

Jamie Symons of Access PaySuite, which compiled the data, commented: "Rising housing costs and living expenses have left many social tenants struggling to maintain rent payments. Our findings show both more households carrying debt and higher average arrears per tenant."

The situation presents significant challenges for local authorities, who must balance rent collection with supporting vulnerable tenants. Experts suggest early intervention strategies could help identify households at risk before debts become unmanageable.

With 228 English councils managing approximately 1.57 million social homes, the growing arrears issue could have substantial implications for local authority finances and their ability to maintain housing stock. The data underscores the need for sustainable solutions that address both tenant affordability and council revenue requirements.

item.title: Prime London house prices fall again as rental market tightens
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Prime London property prices have extended their downward trend, with new data revealing annual declines across both central and outer boroughs. Meanwhile, the capital's rental market continues to tighten, with strong demand pushing rents upwards at their fastest pace in months.

Prime property values decline

According to Knight Frank's latest figures, average prices in prime central London fell 2.1% in the year to October - marking three and a half consecutive years of annual decreases. The outer prime London market also weakened, with values dropping 0.7% over the same period, representing the most significant annual decline since June 2024.

Market analysts suggest several factors are influencing these trends. Higher mortgage costs following global economic uncertainty have particularly affected outer prime areas, where buyers typically rely more on financing. In prime central locations, elevated stamp duty costs and changes to tax regimes for international buyers continue to dampen demand.

Rental market remains robust

The lettings market tells a different story, with rents in prime outer London increasing 3.3% annually - the strongest growth since mid-2024. Current rental values now stand 39% above pre-pandemic levels, reflecting ongoing supply shortages across the capital.

This rental growth demonstrates the resilience of London's property market as an asset class, even as purchase prices face headwinds. Potential landlords might consider these dynamics when reviewing their investment strategies, though it's worth noting that higher borrowing costs could affect yield calculations.

Future market outlook

Industry experts suggest the property market's trajectory may hinge on geopolitical developments and borrowing costs. Some lenders have already begun reducing fixed-rate mortgage products following recent economic shifts, with five-year SONIA swap rates showing notable movement.

Tom Bill of Knight Frank noted that international political developments could influence the UK housing market more significantly than domestic economic announcements. The potential easing of global tensions might help stabilise oil prices and inflation expectations, which could in turn support more favourable mortgage pricing.

While the current market presents challenges for sellers, the relative price stability compared to recent years could offer opportunities for some buyers. Those considering prime London property may wish to monitor mortgage rate trends and global economic indicators closely in the coming months.

item.title: Can landlords charge tenants for damage and cleaning?
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Landlords often face the challenge of properties being returned in a different condition than when first let. Understanding the legal boundaries around charging tenants for damages or cleaning is crucial, particularly under the Tenant Fees Act 2019. This legislation, which applies to England, strictly governs what costs can be passed to tenants – and confusion between 'fees' and 'damages' remains common.

Fees vs Damages: Key Differences

The Tenant Fees Act 2019 makes a clear distinction between prohibited fees and legitimate damage claims:

  • Damages: Landlords may claim for losses resulting from a tenant breaching the tenancy agreement, such as property damage beyond fair wear and tear.
  • Fees: Any fixed charges imposed on tenants for services or specific events are generally unlawful, with only two exceptions – replacement keys and late rent payments (charged at 3% above base rate).

Importantly, landlords cannot impose blanket charges that apply regardless of the property's condition. Any claims must relate to actual breaches of the tenancy terms.

Cleaning Costs: What's Permitted?

Cleaning provides a useful example of how these rules work in practice:

  • Illegal: Fixed cleaning fees in tenancy agreements, regardless of the property's condition when vacated.
  • Permitted: Charging for professional cleaning if the landlord can prove the property was clean at tenancy start and left dirty at end, with costs supported by invoices.

Landlords should note that routine cleaning during a tenancy cannot be charged as a separate fee – any such costs should be factored into the rent. For houses in multiple occupation (HMOs), where regular cleaning may be necessary, this distinction is particularly important.

Making Valid Claims

To successfully claim for damages or cleaning costs, landlords should:

  • Ensure tenancy agreements clearly state tenant obligations regarding property condition
  • Document the property's condition at tenancy start with dated photographs or inventories
  • Keep receipts for any remedial work to demonstrate reasonable costs
  • Distinguish between actual damage and normal wear and tear

The updated government guidance reinforces that landlords cannot use deposits as a general 'slush fund', but may deduct for proven breaches of tenancy terms. With proper documentation and understanding of the rules, landlords can fairly recover costs while remaining compliant with the law.

item.title: Sellers slash asking prices as property industry reacts to latest figures
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

UK homeowners are adjusting their price expectations as shifting market conditions give buyers greater negotiating power. According to the latest Rightmove data, average asking prices dropped by 1.8% (£6,745) in November to £364,270 – a steeper decline than the typical seasonal fall of 1.1%. With mortgage approvals down 20% year-on-year and available properties at a 12-year high, sellers face increasing pressure to price competitively.

Market shifts favour cautious buyers

The current landscape presents challenges for sellers but opportunities for budget-conscious purchasers. Estate agents report that properties perceived as overpriced are spending longer on the market, often requiring subsequent price reductions. Flats in particular face heightened competition as some landlords exit the buy-to-let market, increasing supply in this sector.

Industry experts note that buyers have become more selective, with mortgage affordability constraints shaping their decisions. Tom Bill of Knight Frank observes: "The financial landscape for buyers has become tougher in recent months, with higher borrowing costs causing price growth to stall. This economic backdrop is encouraging sellers to recalibrate their expectations."

Regional variations in market activity

While the national picture shows cooling demand, local markets continue to demonstrate variation. Ben Waterhouse of Waterhouse Estate Agents notes that in South Cumbria and North Lancashire, well-presented homes at realistic prices still attract strong interest. "Buyers are increasingly price-sensitive," he comments, "with ambitious pricing leading to extended marketing periods and tougher negotiations."

The agency has also observed changing behaviour among prospective movers, with more homeowners beginning their property search before listing their current home. This more measured approach suggests a return to pre-pandemic market rhythms, where buyers have greater time to consider options without feeling pressured by intense competition.

As the market continues to rebalance, homeowners considering a sale might benefit from thorough local market research and professional valuations to position their property competitively. With economic uncertainty likely to persist into 2024, realistic pricing and quality presentation could prove crucial in achieving a successful sale.

item.title: New AI tool aims to flag property sale problems before conveyancing begins
item.author: Rizky Aditya Pratama
item.description:
By Rizky Aditya Pratama

Estate agents may soon harness artificial intelligence to spot potential property sale issues before buyers even make an offer. Property tech company Moverly has unveiled its latest innovation, Moverly Connect, which integrates popular AI tools with comprehensive property data to streamline the sales process.

How AI could transform property transactions

The new platform connects AI assistants like ChatGPT and Microsoft Copilot with Moverly's Digital Sale Ready packs, which contain over 300 automated property checks. Rather than manually reviewing every report, agents can now ask the AI to flag listings requiring further investigation. The system scans for common deal-breakers such as absent certificates, restrictive covenants or problematic search results that might otherwise only emerge during conveyancing.

In practice, a branch manager could request their AI assistant to analyse recent listings. The technology would then examine property records, highlight potential red flags with supporting evidence, and even draft preliminary questions for sellers. Crucially, human agents would review all AI-generated content before actioning any communications.

Technical safeguards and industry adoption

Moverly Connect operates using Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open standard enabling AI systems to interface securely with external data sources. This approach allows estate agents to query property information through familiar AI assistants without compromising data security. The system adheres to the Property Data Trust Framework, maintaining strict access controls while facilitating information sharing across the property ecosystem.

The technology builds on Moverly's existing partnerships with major industry players including Lloyds Banking Group and Connells Group, with Skipton Building Society recently joining the network. Through integration with LMS's National Property Transaction Network, agents can seamlessly share upfront property information with conveyancers and lenders, potentially reducing delays later in the process.

Addressing systemic transaction challenges

This development comes as the property sector grapples with persistent transaction fall-throughs and delays. By identifying potential stumbling blocks at the marketing stage rather than during conveyancing, Moverly believes its technology could help stabilise transactions. The company suggests that early detection of issues might allow agents to resolve problems before they escalate, creating a smoother journey for both sellers and buyers.

As AI continues transforming various aspects of the property market, tools like Moverly Connect demonstrate how technology might address long-standing industry pain points. While human oversight remains essential, such innovations could potentially make property transactions more efficient and transparent for all parties involved.

item.author: Sri Wahyuni Astuti
item.description:
By Sri Wahyuni Astuti

UK property sellers are reducing asking prices at a faster rate than seasonal norms as elevated mortgage rates and buyer caution reshape market dynamics. Rightmove's latest data reveals newly listed properties dropped 1.8% (£6,745) in November to £364,270 on average – a steeper decline than the typical 1.1% November falls seen over the past decade.

Mortgage pressures reshape pricing strategies

Persistently high borrowing costs continue to influence both buyer demand and seller expectations. item.title: Tougher tenant checks risk shutting renters out of the market
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

UK renters may face growing challenges securing properties as landlords implement stricter tenant checks and guarantor requirements. Recent research highlights how these tightening standards could inadvertently exclude financially capable applicants from the rental market, particularly young professionals, self-employed workers and international tenants.

Landlords intensify tenant vetting processes

A 2026 landlord survey revealed that 39% of property owners have strengthened their referencing or affordability assessments, while nearly a third have introduced new guarantor requirements. These changes come as the rental sector prepares for the implementation of the Renters’ Rights Act, which will limit landlords’ ability to request large advance rent payments.

Industry experts warn that these stricter measures might create unnecessary barriers for suitable tenants. Tom Tuke Hastings of flatfair commented: "Many renters with stable incomes could find themselves excluded simply because they lack access to traditional guarantors. Not everyone has family members who meet the financial criteria to act as guarantors."

Competitive market compounds rental challenges

The tightening of tenant requirements coincides with intense competition in the rental market. Recent data shows the average rental property now receives over five enquiries, the highest level in two years. This competitive environment means applicants facing additional hurdles from stricter checks might struggle to secure accommodation, even when they can comfortably afford the rent.

Hastings noted: "While landlords rightly seek financial reassurance, the industry must ensure protective measures don’t disproportionately exclude qualified tenants." Some providers now offer alternative solutions, including paid guarantor services, which might help applicants without traditional guarantor options.

Balancing protection with accessibility

As the rental market evolves, stakeholders face the challenge of maintaining landlord protections while preserving tenant access. The upcoming legislative changes may prompt more landlords to rely on guarantor requirements, potentially creating difficulties for certain renter groups.

Industry observers suggest that exploring flexible alternatives to traditional guarantor arrangements could help maintain market accessibility. As Hastings concluded: "The sector needs solutions that safeguard landlords’ interests without creating unnecessary obstacles for responsible renters."

Prospective tenants facing these new requirements might consider researching their options early and preparing necessary documentation to strengthen their applications. Meanwhile, landlords may wish to review their tenant assessment processes to ensure they remain both thorough and fair.

item.title: Housebuilding slump deepens as private construction falls 4.7%
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

The UK’s housebuilding sector has faced a significant downturn, with private construction activity falling by 4.7% in the third quarter of 2026. This decline has contributed to a broader drop in construction output, raising concerns about the nation’s ability to meet housing demand. According to the latest figures from the Office for National Statistics (ONS), the overall construction output fell by 0.7% during the same period, marking a challenging quarter for the industry.

Housebuilding Challenges Intensify

The sharp decline in private housebuilding highlights the ongoing pressures facing developers. Rising borrowing costs and increasing construction expenses have made it more difficult for builders to maintain momentum. Whilst repair and maintenance activity saw a modest increase of 0.5%, it was not enough to offset the significant drop in new housing projects. Additionally, five out of nine construction sectors experienced declines, further underscoring the industry’s struggles.

September did bring a slight recovery, with construction output rising by 0.8% after four consecutive months of decline. New construction work increased by 0.9%, and repair and maintenance activity rose by 0.6%. Infrastructure projects provided the most significant boost, with output growing by 3.3% during the month. However, this monthly improvement was insufficient to reverse the overall quarterly decline, leaving the sector in a precarious position.

Rising Costs and Future Prospects

Despite the challenges, there were some positive signs for the future. Total new orders increased by 1.2% in the third quarter, equivalent to £107 million. This growth was primarily driven by public sector projects outside housing and private commercial construction. However, the rising cost of construction materials continues to pose a significant hurdle. Construction output prices increased by 3.2% in the 12 months to September 2026, adding to the financial pressures faced by developers and contractors.

Phil Hughes, deputy managing director of Paragon Bank SME Lending, commented on the situation: “September’s 0.8% rise in construction output offers some relief after four consecutive monthly falls, with growth across both new work and repair and maintenance. Infrastructure was the main contributor to the monthly increase in new work, which should support demand across the extensive network of SME contractors, equipment providers, and specialist firms.”

Whilst this uptick in infrastructure projects provides a glimmer of hope, the persistent decline in private housebuilding remains a critical issue. With the combination of weaker activity and rising costs, efforts to increase housing supply face significant challenges.

As the industry navigates these difficult conditions, homeowners and prospective buyers may wish to stay informed about how these trends could impact the housing market. Monitoring developments in construction activity and costs could provide valuable insights for those considering their next steps in the property landscape.

item.title: Comings & Goings
item.author: Bambang Setiawan
item.description:
By Bambang Setiawan

Chestertons and Knight Frank have announced key promotions within their London teams, signalling continued confidence in the capital’s prime property market. These strategic appointments come as estate agencies focus on strengthening their expertise in high-value residential sales and international investor relations.

Chestertons expands new homes leadership

Chestertons has promoted Ahmad Alazem to Central London Director for New Homes, reflecting the agency’s commitment to growing its new-build residential business across prime central locations. With five years at the firm and 14 years’ specialism in Middle Eastern investment markets, Alazem will oversee expansion across nine central London branches.

His remit includes developing relationships with property developers, attracting overseas buyers and improving inter-office collaboration. Alazem will continue leading Chestertons’ Middle East and North Africa desk – a role he’s held since mid-2024 – leveraging his extensive experience with international residential investments.

Alazem noted London’s enduring appeal for global investors, particularly from the Gulf region, stating: “With early signs of renewed market confidence, we’re well-positioned to enhance our luxury offerings and connect international buyers with central London opportunities.” Adam Jennings, Chestertons’ head of residential, highlighted Alazem’s “in-depth understanding of prime markets” as key to serving high-net-worth clients.

Knight Frank bolsters Marylebone team

In another senior appointment, Knight Frank has named Daniel Sugarman as head of sales for its Marylebone office – marking a return to where he began his property career in 2018. The promotion follows Sugarman’s recent stint leading core sales in Knightsbridge and his elevation to Partner in 2026.

With 13 years’ London market experience, Sugarman will oversee sales performance and regional partnerships for properties typically valued up to £4 million. His reappointment to Marylebone suggests Knight Frank’s focus on maintaining strong leadership in established prime central London markets, alongside its super-prime operations.

These strategic moves by leading agencies indicate continued confidence in London’s luxury property sector, particularly regarding international investment and premium new-build developments. For prospective buyers, such appointments may signal estate agents’ commitment to providing specialised expertise in competitive central London markets.

item.title: Mortgage arrears fall again – but industry warns worse may be ahead
item.author: Nadya Putri Maharani
item.description:
By Nadya Putri Maharani

UK mortgage arrears have declined for the tenth consecutive quarter, according to the latest industry figures, though experts caution that rising borrowing costs may create future challenges for homeowners and landlords. The data from UK Finance reveals homeowner arrears fell by 10% annually to 76,080 cases in the third quarter of 2026, while buy-to-let arreres dropped more sharply by 22% to 8,170.

However, the figures also show a quarterly rise in property repossessions, with 1,840 homeowner possessions recorded (a 3% increase from Q2) and 690 buy-to-let repossessions (up 10%). Despite these increases, repossession levels remain significantly lower than the previous year's figures.

Experts question whether arrears tell the full story

While the continued decline in mortgage arrears appears positive for the housing market, some industry professionals suggest these figures may conceal underlying financial pressures. Richard Pike of Phoebus Software noted that while falling arrears support market confidence, many households could be facing mounting challenges.

"Higher mortgage costs may take time to fully impact borrowers, particularly those who haven't yet refinanced onto current rates," Pike explained. He also highlighted concerns about rising unsecured borrowing, which might indicate some households are relying on credit to manage daily expenses.

The situation appears most acute for those facing both increased housing costs and changing personal circumstances, such as job changes or family situations. Industry observers suggest lenders are monitoring these trends closely and exploring support options for borrowers showing early signs of financial strain.

Affordability concerns persist across the market

NAEA Propertymark's Ian Harris welcomed the arrears reduction but emphasised that affordability remains a key challenge for both homeowners and property investors. Mortgage costs alongside general living expenses continue to affect buyer confidence and movement within the housing market, he noted.

The buy-to-let sector shows particular signs of pressure, with some suggesting that recent legislative changes, including the Renters' Rights Act, may be contributing to landlords' financial challenges. Mark Harris of SPF Private Clients pointed to the rise in minor arrears cases among landlords as a potential warning sign, though overall levels remain below previous years.

Looking ahead, industry figures stress the importance of maintaining a balanced property market where buyers, sellers and investors can operate with confidence. While current arrears figures offer encouragement, the combination of higher mortgage rates and wider economic factors suggests ongoing vigilance will be needed across the sector.
